lessons.title: ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ (kṣamisi) — forgive me / sorry
lessons.gloss: forgive me / sorry (kṣamisi — imperative of kṣamisu, "to forgive," from Sanskrit kṣamā)

segments.text: You already know ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayaviṭṭu), "please." Kannada's "sorry" reuses a trick you'll see everywhere in this language: taking a Sanskrit noun and turning it into a working Kannada verb.
ಕ್ಷಮಾ (kṣamā) = "patience, forbearance, forgiveness" — a Sanskrit noun, unchanged.

‑ಇಸು (‑isu) = a verb-making suffix: bolt it onto a Sanskrit noun and you get a brand-new Kannada verb. kṣamā + ‑isu becomes ಕ್ಷಮಿಸು (kṣamisu), "to forgive." (The same move builds prārambhisu, "to begin," from Sanskrit prārambha.)
‑ಿ (‑i) = the plain imperative ending — the very one you met on kuḷitukoḷḷi ("please sit") in the please lesson.
So ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ (kṣamisi) is simply "forgive!" — kṣamisu wearing its imperative ending.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: The Dravidian family, side by side

segments.text: Three of the four Dravidian cousins build "sorry" from the very same Sanskrit noun, each with its own verb-making suffix and its own imperative shape:
Kannada ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ kṣamisi — Sanskrit kṣamā + ‑isu (verb) + ‑i (imperative).
Telugu క్షమించండి kṣamin̄caṇḍi — Sanskrit kṣamā + ‑in̄cu (verb) + ‑aṇḍi (imperative).
Malayalam ക്ഷമിക്കണം kṣamikkaṇaṁ — Sanskrit kṣama + ‑ikkuka (verb) + ‑aṇaṁ (necessitative).
Tamil மன்னிக்கவும் maṉṉikkavum — its own native root maṉṉi, not Sanskrit at all.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: about how it's used

segments.text: ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ is a genuine, everyday way to say "sorry" — not overly formal — but in casual conversation you'll also hear the softer ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ ಬಿಡಿ (kṣamisi biḍi, roughly "just forgive [it]") or simply the borrowed English "sorry," which is extremely common in spoken Kannada.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the verb — "kṣamisu," to forgive — then "kṣamisi," forgive!]

segments.text: What is ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ (kṣamisi) built from? (Sanskrit kṣamā "forgiveness".

the verb-making suffix ‑isu + the imperative ‑i.) Which cousin languages do the same trick, and which one doesn't? (Telugu and Malayalam also verb-ify kṣamā; Tamil uses its own native root maṉṉi instead.) What do people often say casually instead? (Kṣamisi biḍi, or simply borrowed English "sorry.")

lessons.title: ಡ (ḍa) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ಡ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach them, but leave these sections until you have stopped: Script you'll notice: ಡ and Guided Practice.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಯ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ಡ — ḍa.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ḍ, it is ḍa.
You already say these, and every one of them has ಡ (ḍa) somewhere inside it:
ಮಾತನಾಡು mātanāḍu — to speak.
ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡು kelasa māḍu — to work (lit. "work-do").
ಎರಡು eraḍu — two.
1. start at the upper left and go down the left side into the left lobe, rising into the middle point.
2. without lifting, drop from the point around the right lobe and climb the right side.
3. without lifting, curl left into the small inner loop and go round it counterclockwise.
4. without lifting, rise out of the loop and close the bowl leftward along the top.
5. lift, then draw the top bar from left to right.
6. without lifting, curl up into the hook.

Pen lifts: 1. The whole body, with the point in its base and the small loop inside its right lobe, is one run that closes along the top; the curled bar comes after the only lift. It is ದ with that small loop tucked inside.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-da.gif', 49 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
The animation is filed as 'da': that series keeps 'da' for this letter, ಡ (ḍa), and spells dental ದ with an h, as 'dha'.

lessons.title: ೧ (1) — the digit for ondu
lessons.gloss: the Kannada digit 1, met on top of a word already learned

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on, your eyes, for letter shapes on the page and your eyes or your hands for the steps that ask you to read, point, write or gesture. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach them, but leave these sections until you have stopped: Script you'll notice: ೧ and Guided Practice.

segments.text: Before the new shape: ಡ (ḍa) — what sound does that letter carry?
You have been counting since you learned to count. Now the written form arrives, one shape at a time.
೧ — 1, the digit for ಒಂದು (ondu), "one".

Kannada writes its numbers with its own ten digits. You will see them on bus boards, house plates and price tags all over Karnataka, sitting beside the Western digits rather than replacing them. Here is the first.
Follow the numbered strip: start where movement 1 begins, and let each panel show you the next movement before your pen makes it. Then write ೧ yourself — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

The strip shows where to start the character and which way to travel, in one attested order. That is taught with real variation from school to school, so the strip names its source beneath it: treat it as a sound way in, not the only one.
